# TLS certificate or host name verification disabled (Python)

`qualor:python/tls-verification-disabled` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-295](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/295.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A07:2025 Authentication Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A07_2025-Authentication_Failures/), [A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A07_2021-Identification_and_Authentication_Failures/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
Code that turns off TLS certificate verification, or the host name check, in an HTTP or TLS
client:

- `verify=False` in `requests` and `httpx` calls, on a `requests.Session` or an `httpx` client;
- `ssl._create_unverified_context()`, and an SSL context with `verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE` and
  `check_hostname = False`;
- `check_hostname = False` on a client context (`ssl.create_default_context()`,
  `ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)`), even when the certificate chain is still checked;
- urllib3's `cert_reqs="CERT_NONE"` and `assert_hostname=False`;
- the legacy `ssl.wrap_socket()` on the client side, which never checks the host name and accepts
  any certificate unless `cert_reqs` asks for one (a socket wrapped with `server_side=True` is not
  reported).

A function that checks the host name itself (`ssl.match_hostname()`) or compares the server's
certificate with a pinned one (`getpeercert(binary_form=True)`) is not reported for a missing host
name check, and neither is urllib3's `assert_hostname=False` next to `assert_fingerprint`.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
Without verification the client accepts any certificate for any host. The traffic is still
encrypted, but to whoever answers: anyone on the network path (a public Wi-Fi, a compromised
router, a proxy) can pose as the server, read the traffic and change it, including passwords and
API tokens.

Turning off only the host name check is not much better: the client then accepts any certificate
its trust store accepts, whoever it was issued to. A public CA issues certificates to anyone for a
domain they control, so an attacker on the path presents their own valid certificate and the
client takes it for the server's.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** verification is switched off to reach a service with an internal CA.

```python
import requests


def fetch_status():
    resp = requests.get("https://internal.example.com/status", verify=False, timeout=5)
    return resp.json()
```

**Compliant:** the internal CA bundle is trusted, and verification stays on.

```python
import requests


def fetch_status():
    resp = requests.get(
        "https://internal.example.com/status",
        verify="/etc/ssl/certs/internal-ca.pem",
        timeout=5,
    )
    return resp.json()
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Keep the default verification.
- To trust a private CA, pass its bundle: `verify="/path/to/ca.pem"` in `requests` or `httpx`,
  `ca_certs=...` in urllib3, or an SSL context from `ssl.create_default_context(cafile=...)`.
- Replace `ssl.wrap_socket(sock)` with
  `ssl.create_default_context().wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=host)`, which checks the
  certificate and the host name.
- Keep `check_hostname` on. To connect by IP address or another name, pass the name the server's
  certificate holds: `server_hostname="internal.example.com"` to `wrap_socket()`, or
  `assert_hostname="internal.example.com"` (or `server_hostname=`) in urllib3. To accept exactly
  one certificate, pin it (urllib3's `assert_fingerprint`).
- For local development, add your development CA to the bundle rather than turning checks off in
  code that may ship.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Requests
- HTTPX
- `ssl`
- urllib3

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- A `requests.Session` that comes from a factory function, another module or a parameter without a
  type annotation is not followed. Sessions made in the same function or module, in a `with` block,
  annotated parameters and `self` attributes set in `__init__` are.
- Options passed as a dict (`requests.get(url, **{"verify": False})`) are not seen.
- `httpx.HTTPTransport(verify=False)`, `getattr(ssl, "_create_unverified_context")`, other
  libraries' switches (boto3 `verify=False`, aiohttp `ssl=False`) and a parameter whose default is
  `False` (`def f(url, verify=False)`) are not reported.
- A bare `ssl.SSLContext()` (without `PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT`) verifies nothing by default, and its use
  as a client cannot be seen where it is made: it is not reported, nor is `check_hostname = False`
  on it, on a urllib3 `create_urllib3_context()`, or on a context made in another function or
  method.
- A function that reads the server's certificate with `getpeercert(binary_form=True)` is taken to
  pin it, whatever it does with the bytes.
- `check_hostname = False` set only when the caller gives no host name (`if not server_hostname:`)
  is still reported.
- `ssl.wrap_socket()`'s `cert_reqs` is read only as written in the call: a variable holding
  `CERT_NONE`, or the number `0`, is missed, and options passed as a dict
  (`ssl.wrap_socket(sock, **opts)`) are reported as if `cert_reqs` were missing.
- An insecure context handed to a server API (`asyncio.start_server(..., ssl=ctx)`) is still
  reported.
<!-- end: known-limits -->
